speakeroldname: Hon. Roger Teillei (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN DISABILITY PENSION RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions both the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board have indicated to members of this house that an adjustment of veterans disability pensions was being taken into consideration in the preparation of the budgetary calculations recently announced.
I have also indicated from time to time that the government was aware of the need for an adjustment of veterans pensions, and that we would not necessarily wait to do this until the two studies we had initiated were completed, that is the Woods committee report and the study of pension rates. It is proposed, therefore, to increase disability pension rates 15 per cent across the board effective January 1, 1S68.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN DISABILITY PENSION RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN DISABILITY PENSION RATES
speechtext: This means, of course, the inclusion of widows, orphans and dependant parents. This will mean an increased expenditure of $30 million in next year's estimates and $7.5 million in this year's expenditures. We will take advantage of the next supplementary estimates to make this effective. Both these increases were taken into account in the estimates of expenditure presented by the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN DISABILITY PENSION RATES

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN DISABILITY PENSION RATES
speechtext:
At least the grave error that was made in November of last year, when the minister said there was to be a 15 per cent increase but it would apply to the basic pension only, has not been repeated. That was a grievous mistake; as a matter of fact veterans with families received the smallest increase. The veterans of the country will not be satisfied until there is a permanent basis for establishing their pension rates. Mr. Speaker, the members of this group are glad to hear the announcement of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) to the effect that veterans will be granted a general 15 per cent increase, without any discrimination as to groups.
However, Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that this presents a contrast with the budget brought down a few weeks ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). Just before Christmas especially, I think that veterans will be very happy about the minister's anouncement.
On the other hand, I call the attention of the minister to the fact that even if we were to grant a general increase of 15 per cent, it would still be desirable, until the measures concerning veterans affairs and allowances are amended, to ensure that no niggardliness is practised as to the degree or percentage of incapacity of veterans. There have been complaints not only on the amount of the pension but also on the procedure to determine the degree of incapacity of a veteran. On this point, I can give many instances of which I am personally aware. I should like to ask the minister at this time to make sure that no niggardliness is shown on this score. It is useless to grant 15 per cent if it is to be taken away in another fashion.
I believe that on consideration of the bill to amend the present legislation, we may deal with this problem and until then, once again, in the name of the veterans, our group welcomes this announcement by the Minister of Veterans Affairs.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN DISABILITY PENSION RATES

Mr. Speaker, I am sure, as has been stated, that veterans across Canada will welcome the announcement that has been made this afternoon, as we welcome it here in the House of Commons. I am also certain that one of the happiest individuals in the house today is the Minister of Veterans Affairs himself, because in spite of the long delay I believe he has been seriously concerned about this particular problem. Not only will his wish be fulfilled, but the minister's announcement will save him from having to answer the many embarrassing questions which are put to him from time to time.
We welcome this announcement, and we know the minister will continue to press for the establishment of an adequate formula for determining these rates. He pointed out that the increased expenditure in the next year's estimates of the department will amount to $30 million, but I believe the people of Canada, in spite of the recommendations of the Minister of Finance to curtail expenditures, will be happy to bear the costs necessary to assist those who served the country so well.

STEEL AND NICKEL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
1.	Does the government Intend providing any support towards increasing the steel and nickel production in Canada?
2.	By how much should this production be increased to meet Canadian requirements?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of State):
subtopic: STEEL AND NICKEL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is concerned: 1. The government already provides substantial encouragement to the nickel and steel industries through certain mineral incentives under the Income Tax Act. These incentives have contributed substantially and directly to past and present expansion programs of these two industries.
2.	Canadian production of nickel far exceeds domestic Canadian requirements, so much so that about 97 per cent of production must be sold on the export market. Canadian steelmaking capacity is now over 12 million tons a year, more than enough to meet current Canadian requirements of about 10.5 million tons a year.
In so far as the Department of Industry is concerned: 1. The government does not currently have any intention of providing support toward increasing steel or nickel production in Canada.
Both of these industries are in a strong position with the exception of the current problems involving the Sydney, Nova Scotia steel plant. There has been a substantial expansion in Canadian plant capacity in recent years.
2.	The Canadian steel industry supplies approximately 87 per cent of the country's demand for primary iron and steel products and in 1966 exported more tonnage than Canadian steel consumers imported. Some of the imports consisted of kinds of steel not produced in Canada.

speechtext:
1. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics collects information from companies, establishments, organizations and individuals, compiles and publishes the resulting data, under the authority of the Statistics Act, chapter 257, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952.

In addition, the dominion statistician is responsible for the administration of the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, chapter 26, 10-11 Elizabeth II which came into force on January 1, 1963. Under this act certain corporations and labour unions are required to supply the dominion statistician with financial and other information.

Under the Statistics Act, section 35, every person who, without lawful excuse, refuses or neglects to answer, or wilfully answers falsely, any question requisite for obtaining any information sought in respect of the objects of the act is guilty of an offence and is liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months or to both fine and imprisonment.
Under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, section 6(1), every corporation that fails to file with the dominion statistician a return for a reporting period as and when required, is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding fifty dollars for each day of such default. Where a corporation is guilty of an offence, every officer, director or agent of the corporation who directed, authorized, assented to or acquiesced in or participated in the offence is a party to and guilty of the offence and is liable on summary conviction to the above fine for the offence or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or to both such fine and imprisonment, whether or not the corporation has been prosecuted or convicted therefor.
3.	Under the Statistics Act, Section 6, every officer, census commissioner, enumerator, agent and other person employed in the execution of any duty under this act must take and subscribe an oath, swearing that he or she will not disclose or make known any matter which comes to his knowledge by reason of his employment.
Under Section 15, no individual return and no part of an individual return made, and no answer to any question put, shall, without previous consent in writing of the person or the owner for the time being of the undertaking, be published, nor, except for the purposes of a prosecution under this act, shall any person, other than a person employed by the bureau, or working under arrangement with the bureau and sworn under the above-mentioned oath, be permitted to see any such individual return, part or answer. In addition,

no report, summary of statistics or other publication under the Statistics Act shall contain any of the particulars comprised in any individual return so arranged as to enable any person to identify any of the particulars as relating to any individual person or business. Returns of carriers or public utilities, hospitals, institutions, libraries and universities are exempt from the secrecy provision except returns of a financial nature or where an individual patient or other person might be identified.
Under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, financial and certain other information is privileged and is available only to an official or authorized person employed for specified purposes. If any such person, including any person formerly employed, contravenes the secrecy section of the act, section 14(7), he or she is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or both such fine and imprisonment.

Sometimes it is suggested that as M.P.'s we have no right or responsibility to criticize the C.B.C. Perhaps I am mistaken, but this seemed to be the tenor of the remarks of the hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond. This is an absurd suggestion. The C.B.C. is a public enterprise, established by parliament and largely financed by the taxes paid by the people. The people know this. They send us their views. We agree with them. We state them.
We do not criticize the private networks. We would not need to, even if we thought we had the right, which of course we have not. The private networks and stations have to please the people in order to live. They live on advertising revenues, which would soon disappear if the people disliked the programs. Do you ever remember seeing a program like "Waiting for Caroline" or "The Paper People" on the private networks? Of course not. The people do not want them and will not pay for them. Therefore the private networks do not show them.
But the C.B.C. gives us such programs, although they offend the sensibilities of the great mass of our people, that great mass of solid, moral, law-abiding citizens which constitutes the strength of this nation. Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by doing something that was not done earlier, and that is to wish a happy birthday to the minister who is responsible for this bill. I want to assure her that, in the interest of giving her a birthday present, I will not impede the passage of this bill, and I hope everyone else will do the same.
However, there are a number of things that I would like to say in a general way in connection with this legislation. The first of them is to commend the minister and those who are responsible for the legislation because I think it can be said in a general way that this is the best piece of broadcasting legislation we have had. It is far better than any of its predecessors, and I think also it is a justification for the substantial amount of time and planning that went into the various factors in the consideration of the bill before it was finally brought into this chamber.
I think the minister would be the first to agree, however, that the legislation has a
December 20, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting great many weaknesses, and that they are almost inevitable and unavoidable for the very reason that broadcasting is unlike any other area of governmental or parliamentary activity when an attempt at control is required. I do not think it is necessary to go into detail as to why this is so, but of course we are dealing in broadcasting with creative forces, and wherever creativity is involved there are bound to be legitimate differences of opinion.
As I said in commenting at the time the resolution was introduced, any of us who are so naive as to believe that legislation will give us good broadcasting are bound to be disappointed. There is of course another reason why legislation in the broadcasting field must of necessity have many shortcomings, and that is the fact that we are also dealing with what is essentially a means of communication. I believe that today there is general agreement, which perhaps did not exist a decade or so ago, that broadcasting is for all practical purposes an extension of the press, in the modem sense of that term. It is a news medium and a medium of information as well as one of enlightenment and entertainment, and whenever the state involves itself, albeit of necessity, in the broadcasting field, it is in fact getting itself involved in something which has an effect on public attitudes and public opinion.
So we have a situation where, despite the best efforts of legislators-and may I say as an aside that I was impressed by the nonpartisan attitude of the broadcasting committee in debating this bill-any form of bill relating to broadcasting has to be inadequate on that account. I myself, perhaps based on my experience, am not as sanguine as some hon. members, perhaps including even the minister, about the efficacy of this bill to resolve the problems which now exist in Canadian broadcasting. I can understand, and perhaps share to a degree, the belief that good men in positions of importance which this bill assigns to them can do a great deal to iron out the differences and the various controversies that have developed. However, at the same time I think it must be said that there is bound to be a continuation of these controversies and difficulties, and the best will in the world will not solve all of them.
One of the things that we have tended to do in this parliament and that has been done throughout the country has been to be rather critical, and perhaps on occasion justifiably

so, of those who up to now have held positions of importance either on the regulatory side or within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. But as one who has had some experience in working with the chairman of the Board of Broadcast Governors and with the former president of the C.B.C., I want to say that I do not know of any two more dedicated men in the country. While inevitably they became the subject of a good deal of criticism, and while inevitably there were those of some competence in broadcasting who on occasion might have taken decisions different from those taken by these gentlemen, I do want to say that I believe Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, for example, deserves a great deal of credit and has given good service to the people of Canada over a great many years. I want to wish him a well earned retirement.
I also want to say a few words of commendation, because they appear to be so rare these days, for the chairman of the Board of Broadcast Governors, and by and large for the actions of that board over the past several years since it was established. It is always easy to pick out those points in the decisions of the board on which there can be criticism and argument, but anyone who is close to broadcasting knows that for every one that has been contentious there have been dozens and indeed hundreds of decisions which have been sound and which on balance, I am sure hon. members would agree, produced the best over-all system of broadcasting of any country of comparable size and geographic and language difficulties in the world. I should like to go on record as saying that the two gentlemen to whom I have referred, and many of their associates, can take a great deal of credit for this achievement.
We are in a situation where the president of the C.B.C. has retired and where from all accounts we are to have two new top executives as soon as this legislation is passed. I am inclined to share the concern and fear of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, who spoke last night about the fact that despite the undoubted talents of the two men who, it is rumoured, will be appointed to the positions, neither of them has any practical experience in the broadcasting field. I believe this will create for them quite serious difficulties, and it will certainly be vitally important that they get from those who are now in the corporation in both high and low level positions full co-operation and a willingness to help them in every way they can,
December 20, 19B7

not only to administer the corporation properly but to acquire the basic knowledge which will be so essential if they are to carry out the mandate implicit in this legislation.
The fact that the two main positions within the corporation will be held by newcomers, whether or not they be in fact the gentlemen whose names have been mentioned, makes it absolutely vital in my view that there be some continuity in the higher echelons of the broadcasting regulatory authority. Having said a few moments ago that I believe Dr. Andrew Stewart has done a good job, and having heard recently of his wish, which I gather has been expressed officially, to retire soon from the position of chairman of the Board of Broadcast Governors, I urge the government to take the steps necessary to try to retain the services of Dr. Stewart at least during the transitional period. I predict that we will have an absolutely chaotic situation in Canadian broadcasting from the administrative and regulatory point of view if we suddenly find that there has been a total and complete change in the top management of the regulatory bodies.
There are a number of specific areas in this legislation to which I should like to refer, and I will do so briefly because I do not intend to make additional comments, in the interest of trying to get this legislation through quickly. But there are three or four comments I should like to make on provisions which I would like to see improved in this bill, and which I commend to the minister either for direct action by amendment in some form or other or for clarification purposes. One of these has to do with whether or not the C.B.C. per se is on all four with the wording in the legislation concerning the objectives of the national broadcasting service. Here I am referring to that portion of the legislation which states rather emphatically that if there is a conflict at any time between private interests in broadcasting and the objectives of the national broadcasting service, they must be resolved in favour of the national broadcasting service.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
During the committee study on this bill I asked the minister whether or not this meant that in any argument between private and public broadcasting the C.B.C. point of view should and must automatically prevail. I suggested then, and I suggest now, that it is a mistake to believe, and some of the comments made in this chamber in recent days

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting confirm my view, that we should automatically equate the C.B.C. as a corporation with the national broadcasting service, or even with the public interest. In other words, it is wrong to assume that the C.B.C. and the public interest are always on all fours. I would ask the minister, if it is not possible to change this wording, which I personally do not like particularly, if she would give assurance to this house that the new council, as it is now to be called, will not automatically be required under the words found in this legislation, automatically to make a decision where a conflict arises in favour of the C.B.C.
I believe there are many cases where it will be perfectly easy to demonstrate that the C.B.C's case is not necessarily one that is automatically in the public interest.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that no one is more aware than the minister of the inevitable difficulties which are going to be encountered in the immediate future. These are going to mushroom over the next three or four years because of the intentions set out in this bill in terms of describing a broadcast undertaking. I am aware of course of the reason that cable television systems, for example, have been embraced within this bill. Having held conversations with certain television operators in the cable field and others, I can understand the degree of their concern over the intentions expressed here.
However, I am not so much concerned as perhaps some other members are about the immediate or direct application of this legislation to cable T.V. systems. I think that they will be able to live with it. I think some form of integration between conventional broadcasting and cable systems is the answer if we are going to direct the whole of broadcasting. The end result of any form of activity of this sort by C.A.T.V. or conventional system is, of course, indistinguishable so far as the viewer is concerned.
There is no doubt that some of the activities in the cable field could have an economically detrimental effect in so far as free television is concerned. What I feel is going to be far more important, and what raises many questions, including constitutional questions, is the developments which are going to occur in the electronics field over the next four or five years, some of which are already evident in certain parts of this country. Only a week or so ago some of the most responsible engineering authorities both in the United States and Canada seriously raised the question at a broadcast symposium as to why
December 20, 1S67

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting we should use the spectrum at all. There is a strong and growing body of conviction that the day will come when broadcasting will cease to use the spectrum in the conventional fashion we are employing it today. In fact, in the great majority of cases, with the possible exception of satellite transmission, the whole of television and the whole of broadcasting will be carried by cable or some means which does not make any use of the air waves.
I suggest that the authorities here will have really grabbed a tiger by the tail if they attempt constantly to modify and change legislation in order to try, and it will be a futile effort, to bring all of these various forms under some form of national or governmental control. I caution those who are going to have this responsibility against this pitfall, whatever I may think or whatever other members may feel about the validity of the present definition of a broadcast undertaking.
I could go on at considerable length to express my doubts about the appeal procedure or the referral procedure that has been included in this bill with regard to matters which are originally approved by the new council and subsequently referred to the governor in council. I will merely content myself with saying that I believe this section is going to be very difficult to work, and that it is going to create all manner of problems for those who must make a decision. The council is established as the licensing authority. The decision of the council must be referred to the governor in council, and it can then be referred back to the council. If it so desires, the council can sustain its original decision. However, the governor in council can then decide not to act on the council's ruling and decision. It seems to me that this is really a shuttlecock operation which is not going to operate very satisfactorily in the long run. If there were more time, a more reasonable way, a better way to get at this problem might well be divised.
The proposal to establish a $100,000 fine for a breach of the regulation is a totally unrealistic and meaningless proposal. I suggest it ought to be removed. I suggest this for a number of reasons. In the first instance, the presence of this figure in the bill tends to suggest that broadcasters, be they public or private, have some sort of capacity for a kind of massive defiance of the public will or the laws of the land. I do not believe this is true. The minister said, in her comments before the committee, that the vast majority of

breaches of regulations which have occurred have been inadvertent and, in her view, action should not have been taken at all. I, for one, cannot visualize a breach of a regulation which would in any way command this kind of economic suicide, and really that is what it would be for a broadcaster to risk this kind of fine.
In my view, what is more ridiculous is that in the back part of this bill, which covers radio, we find the fine is something like $2,500 for a person who sends out a false s.o.s. distress signal to ships at sea. Surely there is nothing that anyone could conceive of in terms of the conventional responsibilities of broadcasters that would warrant a $100,000 fine, when a man in radio can send out false distress signals or commit other offences equally severe and face a potential fine of something like $2,500. Everyone who has appeared before our committee, everyone who has expressed an opinion on this, has agreed that the figure is meaningless. They all agree that no magistrate or judge, under any circumstances, would be liable to impose a fine anything like this figure. I suggest that it is an amount that is rather meaningless and therefore cannot be justified. It will not convince broadcasters, be they public or private, to come along in the fashion and with the encouragement that is the whole reason behind this bill.
There are only one or two other matters on which I want to comment, although I should like very much to deal with the subjects raised by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke last night. I do want to say I feel there is definite improvement in this bill, in so far as the regulation of political broadcasting is concerned. I, for one, do not think the bill goes far enough. It seems to me that in this day and age we ought to regard broadcasting as we regard any other form of mass media. We cannot control the newspapers. There would be a great howl if we attempted to do so, and properly so, in so far as political material is concerned.
I see no reason why the broadcast media should not be treated in precisely the same fashion as the other media. May I recall for the benefit of members that I was one of three on a committee, the other two being the heads of the C.B.C. and the B.B.G., who brought in precisely that kind of recommendation. If we cannot go that far, if there is not a sufficient amount of enthusiasm for my view to permit us to do this, then I think the improvements which are envisaged in this bill are very much worth while.
December 20, 1967
We have recommended that the so-called ban on political broadcasting be reduced to a period of one day rather than two. We have allowed the new authority to give more latitude in the presentation of political broadcasts which surely we all agree, whatever our political convictions, are the dullest material on the air these days. We have eliminated some of the restrictions which were in the old legislation.
One of the things, of course, which is going to be watched most closely by parliamentarians in the next little while is whether or not we are still going to have placed before us these controversies in the broadcasting field with which we are still incapable of dealing. This will depend very largely on whether the machinery established for the resolution of differences between the C.B.C. and the new Canadian radio and television council is effective. Here again, I am not convinced that any commission can resolve these. In some cases they will inevitably involve matters of principle, difficult issues. I do not envy a responsible minister, indeed I do not envy any parliamentarian sitting in this house because I say we are going to continue to have these hot potatoes placed in our laps. I think we ought to examine this matter much more carefully and be prepared, if it does not work, to bring in the necessary amendments.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The real reason that this situation exists, it seems to me, is that we are still not prepared-and this is not a matter that has been raised by only those on one side of the house; it seems to be something that is believed by numbers of members in all parties-to say what ought to be said, and that is that the Canadian radio-television council is the ultimate authority and that the C.B.C. is responsible to it. There are many instances throughout the legislation where an "out" is provided for the C.B.C., and unless my guess is very wrong and my experience taught me nothing we are going to see the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation taking advantage of these "outs" on every occasion when they can get elsewhere what they are looking for from the C.R.T.C. Therefore I say once again that the day must come when the C.B.C. is made subject to this authority in the same way as other broadcasters.
Further, Mr. Chairman, may I say we simply cannot deal with this matter in its totality until we see the financing bill which is going to follow this one, and which will set
5679
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting up the system under which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is going to be financed. When that day comes, which I presume will be early in the new year, we will have to examine carefully whether the various assignments given the corporation are justified in relation to the very large sums of public money which we will be asked to expend.
I also believe, Mr. Chairman, that there is a great need to examine the whole concept of statutory grants. Personally I believe in this principle, but I contend it will be meaningless unless the C.B.C. are told clearly and emphatically, having been given a certain amount of money, that they will have to live within their means. If there is again a loophole which enables the corporation to come back annually or whenever they feel like it to change their so-called statutory grant, then the financial control over the corporation will be no better than it is today, and conceivably could be worse. Therefore the next stage in this important debate will be when we receive the financing bill.
Having filed these reservations, Mr. Chairman-and some may regard them as serious reservations-I still say that this is a good bill. As the minister has stated, it will depend a good deal for its implementation on the wisdom, the sense of responsibility and the awareness of those who are given the important jobs on the council and in the corporation. However, I do not believe that we have yet reached the stage-and I wish we had on this eve of Christmas, 1967-when we can say that parliament can at last free itself from a role for which it is really not suited, which is acting as a day to day arbiter of public taste in the functioning of our broadcasting system.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, what I have been trying to say up to now is that the criticisms that we hear are valid. But let them not blind us to the fact-and anybody who has seen television and listened to radio programs in other countries I feel would have to agree-that Canada is served extremely well by its broadcasting system today. By that I mean both the corporation and the private elements. I hope that this bill will enable all of us to serve Canada even better.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments with regard to clause 2 of Bill No. C-163. My first remark

5680	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting deals with subclause (b) of clause 2 which reads as follows:
(b) that the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to preserve and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economical fabric of Canada;
However, Mr. Chairman, it so happens that, in Canada, several radio and television stations are operated while the majority of their shareholders are not Canadian citizens nor Canadian residents but American citizens, which is contrary to legislation.
I should like to refer, as an illustration, to the two television stations in Quebec: channel 4 and channel 5 which are not owned by Canadian citizens. In answer to a question which I had put on the order paper, the hon. Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) said that those two television stations operated under an order in council. In Quebec, there are three television stations, the C.B.C. and two private stations owned by American interests.
Mr. Chairman, I think that the hon. Secretary of State will admit that it is an abnormal and unacceptable situation. The present legislation, even before it was amended, specifies that our radio and television broadcasting stations must be owned by Canadian citizens.
In subclause (b) of clause 2 it is clearly stated, and I quote again:
(b) that the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians
In Quebec, the only two private television stations are owned by American subjects. The result is that those two television stations present regularly news commentaries, three times a day on the French station and three times a day on the English station, and they are identical commentaries, translated back into English, since those two stations are owned by the same American company. When comments are made on a decision taken by the federal government or by the Quebec government or by a municipality, it is always the American point of view which is put forward during the news commentaries of those two Quebec stations, either the English or the French station. It is always the American point of view on, or reaction to, the events occurring in Canada and Quebecers, as a result, are overwhelmed by American reactions.
I think this is not at all normal, since an attempt is being made to have Quebecers think or figure according to what the Americans think, because these editorials of the

DEBATES	December 20, 1967
two Quebec television stations are prepared according to American ideas or reactions since such stations belong to Americans.
There is a young squirt who reads these editorials, possibly with some assurance, but everyone knows that he is not writing them; nevertheless, they are regularly given over the Quebec television, either on the French station or on the English station.
So, Mr. Chairman, I believe that the former legislation stated that television and radio stations in Canada "should belong to Canadians." The new legislation restates it, but the cabinet passes orders in council, allowing the operation of the two Quebec stations even though they are owned by American citizens. I wonder if the Secretary of State accepts this situation. I believe, in the circumstances, that subclause (b) should be amended so that it will no longer provide that:
-the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians-
-but read as follows:
-the Canadian broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
No longer "should", because that is a statement of good intentions achieving nothing. What we need is to write the principle firmly and precisely in the legislation thus:
The Canadian broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians-
Further, the minister should grant a maximum delay of a few months to require these American concerns to sell the shares they own in these two Quebec television stations. I believe this is completely normal since the minister, when drafting her bill, admits that "the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned by Canadians." Why not then clarify the principle and include it in the legislation by providing that "the Canadian broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians"?
Then, the good intentions of the minister would be written in the legislation and the owners of such companies would have a fixed period to sell their shares on the Canadian market. It would be easier as barely two or three years ago-three years I think-when the B.B.G. granted a licence for the operation of a C.B.C. television station in Quebec city, some Quebecers had applied for a licence to operate a private station there. Therefore, since some Quebecers are interested in private television in Quebec city, why
December 20, 1967	COMMONS
leave it under the control of American citizens?
The fact that the minister mentioned subclause 2 shows her good intentions; but this does not go far enough, and I feel the bill should be much more specific. That is why I intend to move an amendment to clause 2(b). Therefore, I move:
That subclause 2 (b) be amended by substituting, in line 11, the word "shall" for the word "should".
so that the amended paragraph would read as follows:
-the Canadian broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to preserve and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada;
Therefore, I move that amendment and I would ask the Secretary of State to accept it, since her views and good intentions are already known with regard to the Canadian ownership of our radio and television stations.
I submit that amendment, trusting that the Secretary of State will readily accept it. At the same time, she could perhaps tell us, indeed assure us, that her department will see to it that, as soon as possible private radio and television stations controlled by foreigners are handed over to Quebec interests, and that those foreigners sell their shares on the Canadian market.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some general remarks about the C.B.C. and broadcasting in Canada. We have had a broadcasting system in Canada for about 30 years now and many who look closely at that system say that it has failed to carry out its initial and primary purposes. On the other hand, when some of us realize that certain milestones in broadcasting have been passed, we are satisfied with some progress that has been made so far.
I think every member of parliament receives many letters criticizing the extremes of programming content of certain C.B.C. programs. Some of the feature programs particularly, which are said to reflect the changes taking place in our society, have been found objectionable by some. In our society the population has been moving from 27053-358i
DEBATES	5581
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting urban to rural areas. Those who live in rural Saskatchewan, as well as those who live in the urban areas of that province, find it hard to believe that some C.B.C. programs reflect the realities of Canadian life today.
The members of this parliament and of future parliaments will be charged with the responsibility of directing the broad stream of broadcasting in our nation in the years ahead. Since we endow producers and directors of programs with great responsibilities, they should be Canadian citizens, especially when they work within the C.B.C. I do not know how many of them are not Canadians but I have been told that in the administrative hierarchy there are some who cannot claim Canadian citizenship. I believe that a corporation like the C.B.C. or any crown corporation which is involved with the objectives that are set forth in this legislation, should be staffed at senior levels with citizens of this country. Those citizens should have a true interest in pursuing objectives that are national, and peculiar to this nation.
I feel that the way we allocate our broadcasting stations in Canada enables some to obtain greater privileges than others. Some of those privileges are much more valuable than we thought they would be a few short years ago. Those stations which have been established should be more strictly supervised than they have been. I say that because I can think of one or two staions which have almost become a law unto themselves. They wield a tremendous influence in certain areas of the country. The course they pursue with regard to national objectives is questionable.
I believe, sir, that Canada has room for more television stations than she has presently; primarily, I am speaking of privately owned television stations. Stations should not be given a monopoly in the area they serve. I recognize that new stations must establish themselves if they are to become a strong factor in the communications media of an area. Yet I believe that other stations should be allowed in areas which are already served by an existing station. I think that those who grant licences ought to be freer with their allocations than they have been in the past. Competition will not hurt our broadcasters; it may raise the over-all tone of broadcasting in this country.
When I said that producers and directors ought to be Canadian citizens, I did not mean necessarily that the artists who appear on the C.B.C. must be Canadians. Obviously, artists from other countries are welcome to take
5682	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting part in some programs. But the top administrators and the more important producers and directors of the C.B.C. ought to be Canadians. I must impress on the minister the necessity of making certain that Canadians have a voice in what programs are to be broadcast in this country.
The hon. members for Saskatoon and Kindersley have asked for television stations to be established in their areas. The hon. member for Saskatoon especially, for the past year or two, has asked for a television station to be established in Saskatoon. Demands have also been made for a French television station to be set up on the prairies, though, as I understand, the advent of such a station is some way off. Past legislation has decreed that there be English and French networks in Canada, but as I look at Saskatoon I cannot see that a French television station in that area has any prospect, at the present time, of paying its way. Where a limited number of French speaking people live on the prairies, radio or television stations in the area might carry programs in English and French. This would be possible if there were other stations in the field in these areas; their presence might go a long way toward ending some of the difficulties we have encountered. I cannot but feel that some action is needed in Saskatoon either to provide a C.B.C. outlet or to allow private individuals to provide one. If Canada does not intend to spend any more money to set up television stations, then surely we should consider allowing others to provide them if they are willing to make the necessary funds available.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This leads one to the whole question of whether the C.B.C. should be in the station business at all. I realize it is a little late to bring up this point now, nevertheless, when one considers the amount of money involved in setting up a station and the lucrative possibilities which such stations present today we are bound to reflect on the fact that we have seen nothing but deficits in the C.B.C. accounts year after year, and that the forecast for the future is unchanged. The prospect is surely one which encourages us to consider whether we are justified in providing funds for the setting up of stations by the C.B.C., possibly at the expense of assistance which might develop the talents of Canadian artists and give them a real incentive.
To my mind, the development of Canadian talent is one of the great problems facing television in this country. I think the failure to develop our own talent adequately is one

DEBATES	December 20, 1967
of the reasons we have so many poor programs from the C.B.C. today. We have asked the corporation to seek out Canadian talent. In many instances its efforts have been found lacking, and as a result some of the programs have been vulgar, lacking in taste, even shocking to a great many people. It seems that programs of this kind were the only ones which could be relied upon to draw attention, at C.B.C. headquarters. This forces us to ask what qualifications are set by officials in senior positions when they determine who are to produce and direct the programs which go on the air.
I do not believe any easy solution will be found. We still have a long way to go. The federal government, together with provincial governments should devote more attention to providing incentives for the development of real artistry-the creation of a pool upon which the C.B.C. could draw. It is my belief that as a result of the way in which the two networks have been set up in Canada there has been an overwhelming inclination to draw talent from the corporation's centres in Montreal and Toronto.
Talent which might be developed in the outlying parts of Canada has been overlooked to some degree, though I am firmly of the opinion that talent exists in many parts of this country outside Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa. I do concede that it needs encouragement and development. I would go further and say there is a useful field of work open here for some agency of the government, some segment of the C.B.C. itself.
Before going further I wish to congratulate the minister on her birthday today we could make that unanimous, all round the house.

I have been listening with interest to the speeches which have been made during this discussion. I was particularly interested in what was said by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, because of his background in the medium now under consideration. I do not intend to comment on his speech in any detail, but I will say I agree with him when he says that the officials who have just retired or who are about to retire from the corporation and give up their responsibilities in this field certainly served as public servants to the best of their ability during a tumultuous period in the history of broadcasting. To this extent we owe them our appreciation for their efforts.
I was also interested in the speech made last night by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke. I was surprised he appeared to be so diffident about raising the question he dealt with at that time. Perhaps it was only the lateness of the hour which caused him to express himself as he did when he told us he intended to discuss the undiscussable, namely the question of good taste in broadcasting. I have never felt that this is a subject about which one should be inhibited in any way when speaking, and I should like to make reference to the hon. member's proposal for dealing with this problem. Let me refer to his remarks as they appear at page 5648 of yesterday's Hansard, where he had this to say:
I would suggest that In the final stage of considering the legislation we should give serious thought to amendments which will set down a little more firmly guide lines for the Canadian radio television council not only for C.B.C. broadcasting but also in the private area, because I think it is important for us not to abdicate this great responsibility.
I am not quarrelling with the objective the hon. member had in mind, nor am I quarrelling with his remarks critical of certain programs. Indeed, I shall myself have some critical things to say about some programs before I conclude. However, I do not subscribe to his idea that one can legislate good taste. As far as the bill is concerned, the guide lines laid down in it appear to be fair and sensible. I believe the question of good taste in broadcasting is something which has to be left in the hands of those who operate the broadcasting system, subject to the reaction of the Canadian people and in particular of this parliament.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This brings me to a point I would like to raise for the consideration of the committee.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting It is that in this bill we have not in any way touched on a very important aspect of this whole matter, the relationship to parliament of the broadcasting system and the Canadian radio television council. Often over the years that I have been a member of this house I have heard the idea expressed that the broadcasting system and its operation were responsible to parliament, and not to the government. While there has been lipservice paid to this idea, it really seems to me that this question of the relationship to parliament has never been defined, has never really been dealt with in a way that created a satisfactory situation.
In dealing with this piece of legislation which, as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo said, most members consider to be a forward step, I think we should give some attention to this aspect of the matter. I for one have never felt that the arrangement, whereby one of the ministers of the crown acts as spokesman or go-between betwixt parliament and the Board of Broadcast Governors and the C.B.C., has been a satisfactory one. The desultory questioning on orders of the day and the assurances given by the responsible minister that he or she would bring an hon. member's remarks to the attention of the president of the C.B.C., or what-have-you,. have been so unsatisfactory that in some ways they have been responsible for a lot of the general discontent with the operation of the broadcasting system in recent years.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I would like to add that in my view the various ministers who had that responsibility during the time I have been a member of the house, including the days when the late Dr. McCann was minister of national revenue and played that role, and when the late former member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, who was also minister of national revenue, played that role, all were most meticulous in trying to maintain the attitude that the broadcasting system was not the tool of the government but was responsible to parliament. The present minister has very meticulously given the same kind of response when members of this parliament have put questions to her.
There has been some reference to some of the present minister's comments, as an individual member or citizen, with respect to certain aspects of the management of broadcasting. Indeed there has been some furore about her comments. I would remind the committee that this is not a unique situation. I recall that when a number of years ago the
December 20, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent led the government an occasion arose when there was an extended debate in the house about whether he, the prime minister, could make a representation to the president of the C.B.C. as a private citizen.
It is for this reason, as well as taking into consideration the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, that we should seek to legislate in more detail the matter of programming, in relation to whether it is in good taste or bad taste, whether it is poor programming or good programming, that I wish to put forward the view that we in this chamber ought to be giving some serious thought to another way in which we could express our views on the question of broadcasting.
If the concept of the responsibility of parliament as an institution for the operation of broadcasting, rather than of the government, is to have any real meaning, then this national forum should set up some kind of machinery or mechanism of its own through which, from time to time, members could channel the views of their constituents, as well as their own views on the nature of various programs. When the hon. member for Kindersley was speaking he tried to imply that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond suggested we did not have any right to criticize C.B.C. programming. That was not my understanding of the remarks made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond. But what did strike me, if I heard it correctly, was the comment by the hon. member for Kindersley, that there was some distinction between our right as members of parliament to criticize C.B.C. programming and to criticize programming carried by privately owned stations or network.

Yes, today the Prime Minister complained about a broadcasting matter which, from the context of his remarks, related to a privately owned operation. But this leads me to suggest that the members of the official opposition should make up their minds on whether they support this legislation or not. I would draw the attention of the hon. member for Kindersley and of the hon. member for Rosthern to the very beginning of the clause now under consideration, which sets out, as it has been so often set out in the past, that Canadian broadcasting constitutes a single system and that all persons licensed

to carry on broadcasting have a responsibility for programs they broadcast, but also have the right to freedom of expression.
I would like to put that on all fours with the right of members of parliament to freedom of expression, taking literally the text of this bill which sets up the broadcasting system as a single system. It is on that basis that we should consider our role with respect to what we think programming should be, and with respect to the other activities of broadcasters.
Instead of trying to set out guide lines in detail concerning what is good taste and poor taste, as suggested by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, I think we ought to consider what role we might play in this area, through proper discussion from time to time of broadcasting and its content. I hope to make some critical comments about a certain program if time permits, Mr. Chairman, but I do not feel this is a satisfactory way to do so. While I am trying to make my comments relevant to the bill, certainly as relevant as those of other hon. members have been, nevertheless I would point out that each time a broadcasting bill or financial proposal relating to broadcasting comes before us, we tend to use it as an occasion to criticize programming. This has resulted in rather desultory and undirected discussion about the content of programming.
I think we should consider taking a new approach to the question of the responsibility of parliament for broadcasting. Instead of having a minister as our spokesman or go-between in matters concerning the new Canadian radio-television council, I think we might have Mr. Speaker perform this role, as our spokesman to the C.B.C. and the regulatory body.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
What has given rise to this thought in my mind was the procedure adopted in relation to another aspect of life in this country. I am referring to the procedure laid down in the bill which set up the redistribution commissions. As hon. members will recall, there is provision under the rules for debates on what the redistribution commissions have done. A copy of such debates is sent to the commissions by the Speaker of the house, as an official expression of the views of the members of the house. There is also provision under which the house can give its expression of opinion by way of a resolution. It does seem to me consideration might be
December 20, 1967

given to something, perhaps not exactly parallel but somewhat similar to that, in connection with the matter of broadcasting. This could be done without any direct relationship to the bill. It could be done by an arrang-ment under our rules whereby from time to time there could be a motion "that this house express its opinion to the C.B.C." or the Canadian council on radio and television. This motion would be debatable and amendable. We could then have a discussion which could be centered on the matter of programming, or the general policy in respect of the extension of broadcast facilities into coloured television or to areas such as referred to by the hon. member for Kindersley, or to that area of the country from which I come. Such a debate would provide proper focus for the expression of the views of members of this house and, through them, the people of Canada.
It seems to me there is a helpless feeling on the part of many Canadians about this business of merely being able to write to their member, who asks a question of the minister, who in turn then says she will draw the remarks to the attention of the proper official, whoever he may be. They can simply write to the C.B.C. and get a reply from the president on matters of programming. I am not suggesting there is no place for this type of comment on programming, but there are times when certain issues develop which should be focused in this house. If there is going to be any real meaning to the concept of the responsibility of parliament for the broadcasting system, some kind of focus of that sort is necessary, and this is something we should do after we have dealt with this bill.
Contingent upon that I think is an acceptance on the part of members of this house of the principles of the broadcasting system as they are set out in this bill. If there have been suggestions that people like myself and the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond have been a little hesitant in our criticism from time to time of the C.B.C., it is perhaps because we have believed as strongly as any in the idea and value of a public broadcasting system. We have been concerned over the years with attempts by members of the Conservative party, although not exclusively, to subvert the concept of public broadcasting, and it seems to me there was an example of that sort of thing in the remarks made last night by the hon. member for Oxford. The same sort of criticism has been expressed much more strongly during previous sessions

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting by hon. members in that part of the house, but I think this is dying out. I hope there will be a recognition of the spirit and the realities set forth in this bill.
The hon. member for Rosthern questioned whether the C.B.C. should operate television stations. His remarks were the echo of something expressed much more strongly during previous sessions by members sitting in that part of the house. It seems to me that if we could bring this out in the open, as a right of parliamentarians during a proper debate, and in some way convey our criticisms of programming to the responsible authorities it might be possible to establish a much more satisfactory relationship between ourselves and the broadcast authorities than obviously has existed in recent years.
Having said that, I must add my share of blood-letting by drawing attention to the sort of thing which I hope will come to an end with the adoption of this bill. I have always felt that if one is going to criticize he should do so specifically and in relation to particular programs or actions. The one I should like to draw to the attention of the house is a program which was of great concern to some of my constituents. It was called "Young in a Small Town", which was carried on "Camera West" August 20 last. This program focused on one of the communities in my constituency. Certainly most of the constituents of that area considered it to be a very unfair portrayal of the situation as it exists.
Let me say first of all that the C.B.C. Times, about which some others have spoken, in describing this program displayed a very cheap and sloppy piece of journalese when, in referring to the Albernis on Vancouver island, it said:
Huge complexes of pulp mills, shingle mills, saw mills, and plywood manufacturing plants dominate the towns with their soaring smoking chimneys and the cacophony of machines

This is just a sloppy and inaccurate piece of writing. Perhaps it would be more accurate if it had referred to a huge complex, because there is one pulp mill, one shingle mill, two saw mills and one plywood plant. Later on it refers to the young people with big cars who roar around the country, and it mentions that the population of this area is approximately 20,000. At another place in this article it states:
Week ends is the time for "blowin' up the gas" and great hordes of these youngsters head for the larger cities of Nanaimo and Victoria on the island or Vancouver on the mainland-
December 20, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
I do not know what the estimate of the producer or the writer of this article would be in respect of great hordes, but it certainly sounds like this means the 20,000 people living in the Albernis roar out of the towns on week ends. The writer might have been more accurate if he had said 50 or 100,-and I have travelled that highway often myself.
I wrote to the president of the C.B.C. about this program. I had to admit that I had not seen it myself but had heard a lot about it from many people. When I became aware of the widespread and official concern of the community, which was expressed by the mayor and the city council as well, to the regional director of the C.B.C., I made a point of carrying out a rather broad inquiry. I said in my letter:
I may say that I did not myself actually view this program, but have had it discussed with me by a great many people who did see it. If I may make my own observation as a result of these discussions, there would appear to be a consensus that the social situation outlined does not exist as an element of the life of the Albemi community and also of many others in Canada today. The main brunt of the criticism appears to have arisen from the fact that it was presented in documentary form, focusing on a particular community and, therefore, in presenting one narrow facet of life in this community on a nationwide hookup, thereby created a very distorted image of what the community actually is.
This was underlined by the kind of blurbs that were written about the program in the C.B.C. Times.
I then said in my letter:
Had the social situation been presented in the form of a play or in some way which did not pinpoint it on a particular community there would, I believe, have been much less valid grounds for objection to the program.
In the reply I received to that letter the comment about the program was completely ignored, and I was told:
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
As you have so aptly observed, the social situation outlined is common to virtually all parts of North America. This is pointed out in the letter which Mr. Caple sent to the mayors of Alberni and Port Alberni-*
With regard to the investigation into the program, in my view either the producer of the program completely brainwashed the regional director of the C.B.C., and through him the president, or they are simply refusing to recognize the incorrect approach taken in the program by pinpointing a particular community in a way that made it appear that the community was involved to a greater extent than any other and completely dis-

torting the situation as far as that area is concerned.
As one of the aldermen of the cities pointed out, the impact of this program was such that someone in Nova Scotia who heard that a friend of his was moving from Alberni to another community wrote saying he was so glad his friend was getting out of this horrible place. This is the kind of distortion to which the people of the Albernis were objecting. They were not denying the existence of a social situation; they were objecting to the form of the program which was carried on a national hook-up and gave the impression that this was the main characteristic of the community. If the community had not been mentioned by name, and the program had televised scenes of the area and used them as a documentary, I do not think there would have been so much ground for criticism.
The latest comment on the matter, as a result of further protest and the suggestion that there be a fresh look at the matter, is that the program was not staged with a view to distorting the situation. In this connection I should like to quote part of an article which appeared in the Nanaimo Free Press of December 15. The article points out that Mr. Caple said that none of the scenes were staged or edited with intent on the part of the C.B.C. to reflect adversely on youth generally in the community. Perhaps the intent was not there, but the fact is that the program did reflect adversely on the community and its youth. The fact is that scenes were staged. There are a number of people in the community who know they were staged and any attempt on the part of the producer, Mr. Caple, or anybody else to deny it is not very convincing.
The people producing the program got two or three high school students, who happened to be driving fairly nice cars, owned by their parents, to go round and round the school in order to create the impression that all the students of the high school were driving this kind of car. The producers provided beer to young people on the beach on the west coast so they could portray them drinking beer on the beach. In view of these facts my constituents cannot be convinced that the program was not staged.
The situation that was portrayed is one that exists; nobody in the community is quarrelling with that. They are quarrelling with the fact that the whole situation was enlarged and distorted to create the impression across the country that this was the
December 20, 1967

main characteristic of the community. This is what the people are objecting to, and it is what I am now objecting to on their behalf. I have made my point-

speakeroldname: Mr. Harold E. Winch (Vancouver East) moved:
subtopic: STUDY BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF CARE, UTILIZATION AND TREATMENT OF ANIMALS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the following matters should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development with the authority to call for persons and papers and report its deliberations with recommendations :
1.	The use of animals for medical research purposes, their care and utilization, and procedures for government licensing and inspection of, and control over, all premises using animals for laboratory research or medical training;
2.	The treatment of animals as pets and, as far as federal jurisdiction permits, recommendations regarding legislation providing penalties for those abusing animals, and any persons making a business of raising or catching animals for sale to research individuals or centres and not keeping the same in a humane manner;
3.	The most humane method of trapping furbearing animals, and consideration as to whether the Canadian seal hunt should, and could on a practicable basis be discontinued; and
4.	Consideration of the entire Canadian picture relative to the maintenance of fish, bird and animal wildlife and the regulations required for conservation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the remarks which I intend to make are based on voluminous files which are the result of one year's intense inquiries and research on the subject matter of this motion, inquiries with respect to which were sent to various countries of the world. Hon. members will have noted that

December 20, 1967
Research
this motion has been on the order paper since May 9, and therefore there has been plenty of time for the purport and the implication of its wording to be studied and understood. I sincerely hope that all hon. members who have read the motion will note that it is not dogmatic in its terms and that it makes no specific recommendation. It outlines serious matters which, in my estimation, are not only worthy of, but demands, the attention of the house and the study, investigation, hearing of representations and recommendations from a select standing committee of the house.
Perhaps there is only one aspect of the motion on which hon. members might wish an explanation, that is the suggestion that the four points contained in it should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture. The reason for this is that on making inquiries and investigations throughout a number of countries in the world I have found that these matters were being always referred for study either to a royal commission or to the agricultural committee of the legislative body of the country, and that when action was taken by the legislative body, the enforcement of regulation and the inspection of the licensing was undertaken by that country's department of agriculture. It is because I have discovered this to be the procedure in other countries of the world, and particularly the United States and the United Kingdom, that I suggested reference of the subject matter of this motion to the select standing committee on agriculture.
First of all I should like to deal briefly with the fourth point in the motion, which is the consideration of the entire Canadian picture relative to the maintenance of fish, bird and animal wildlife and the regulations required for conservation. I am certain that every one in the house is interested in conservation, but wishful thinking, or pious or sanctimonious utterances are not sufficient. We need action, and that action must be taken soon. As a result of research I have discovered that there has been a brutal massacre of wildlife on this continent. In the past 150 years 60 species of birds and animals have been exterminated by the greedy and the ignorant. Experts in the United States and Canada have informed me that about 80 other species of birds and animals are on the danger list and face the same fate. Surely I need only mention what is happening to our big horn sheep, our grizzlies and our polar bears.
Last year we heard about so-called sportsmen using helicopters to locate polar bears

and grizzlies and shooting them from the plane, with the result, the experts say, that these species are dangerously near extinction. So the fact some species of birds and animals are being exterminated is sufficient reason to refer this important matter to the committee for study.
I want to say immediately that I realize that action is required on a federal, provincial and, in some aspects, on an international basis. However, someone must give the lead, and I respectfully ask hon. members this question: Who would be better qualified to give the lead than the House of Commons of Canada? This is the reason for point 4 of the motion.
In the past two years in particular a great deal has been said about seal hunting by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), and we accepted what he had to say. However, experts in the field who have witnessed seal hunts have criticised the way in which they have been carried out. So much has been said and publicised concerning seal hunts that this matter is now of world concern and interest.
I hope all hon. members have noticed that I have not been dogmatic on the subject and have not even taken sides on it. I have been careful not to do this because of the importance of the humane treatment and conservation of animals, the necessity for studying the most humane method of trapping furbearing animals, and consideration as to whether the Canadian seal hunt should, and could, on a practicable basis be discontinued. We will not get a satisfactory answer to questions through asking questions on orders of the day. This should be a matter of study and representation. First let the truth come out, and then let the all-party committee on agriculture make its recommendations on the basis of evidence.
This leads me to points 1 and 2 in my motion which concern the treatment of animals as pets, and their use for medical research. This is without doubt a most controversial matter and one which should be considered without bias and without prejudice. We must recognize the feelings of animals when we consider their use in medical research in an effort to find methods of helping human beings. We have no legislation that governs this in Canada. Many of us, I think all, if they knew the facts, are vitally concerned.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
May I introduce what I have to say on this phase of the subject, Mr. Speaker, by quoting
December 20, 1967

the first paragraph of a submission made to a previous minister of justice. The heading of the submission is "The Protection of Animals Used in Scientific Research," and the paragraph reads:
Medical research has made great strides in recent years, and one of the contributing factors has been the possibility of testing new techniques and materials on animals prior to applying them to human patients. Many people have accepted the use of animals for this purpose in the belief that man is justified in inflicting some suffering on animals if it leads to permanent relief of human suffering. They have assumed, however, that no more pain would be inflicted than was absolutely necessary for the purpose and that the animals would be given all the care and attention they require. Unfortunately, there is overwhelming evidence that this is not always the case.
In these massive files on my desk, Mr. Speaker, I have reports of investigations by the Congress of the United States as well as a report of the departmental committee on experiments with animals, headed by Sir Sidney Littlewood in the United Kingdom. This report was filed in April of 1965. I have magazines, books and reports from many countries of the world which contain material that is absolutely horrifying. We see here irrefutable proof of the unnecessary pain inflicted in the name of human beings. Evidence was given before a committee of the Congress of the United States about three years ago concerning dogs being kept in small cages without exercise for up to seven years; about intermittent electric shock being applied to dogs over a period of six months in order to produce a state of chronic fear. Evidence was given before the royal commission of the crushing of the legs of over 400 dogs in a press, without any anaesthetic from the time of this procedure until death some 24 hours later.
We read that dognapping reached such proportions in the United States that on March 25 last year the house agricultural committee approved legislation aimed at curtailing the activities of dognappers who sell pets to research centres. The bill gives the department of agriculture in the United States licensing powers over persons who sell cats and dogs for research purposes, and over the institutions which buy them. We hear people say that this cannot happen in Canada. However, we have no licensing control; we have no authority and no knowledge of what goes on. According to evidence given to the committee of the United States Congress, over 100 million animals a year are used for medical and scientific purposes in that country alone. In the light of all these facts, I say 27053-3591
Research
this is a matter for investigation by a committee of this House of Commons.
We say it can't happen here, and yet I read this from one of our newspapers:
Officials from the Montreal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals raided a dog kennel Friday near Granby, 40 miles east of Montreal, and brought back 60 dogs only seven of which were expected to live-
The dogs, suffering from hunger, distemper, mange and cuts, were brought to Montreal in three S.P.C.A. ambulances along with two dozen rabbits and chickens.
We read also that 13 year old high school students are using animals for experimental diagnostic purposes. This is right in the record. We have no provision whatever for dealing with the matter. I know there may be conflicting jurisdiction, provincial, federal and international, but someone must take the lead. I can think of no better source of leadership than this House of Commons referring the study of this matter to a committee. The committee could study the use of animals in medical research in our country, study whether or not there should be licensing and inspection by federal or provincial authorities, not only of those who catch or raise these animals for research but also of the; universities or laboratories that use them.
We have the right, sir, because the animals feel pain, to have an interest and concern in every phase of animal protection, animal use and the conservation of our wildlife. In this way, members may receive the benefit of representations made to the committee, receive knowledge of the use of animals and what we can possibly do about it.
I am not going to speak any longer, except to say this: In the past two or three weeks I and other members interested in this matter have done our best to obtain the opinions of other members. We have yet to find one who does not agree that this is a matter worthy of study or worthy of reference to a committee. I conclude my remarks therefore in the hope that since the motion is not dogmatic, but merely asks for a study, that it will be accepted by all members.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit that having given the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) quite a bit of consideration before rising to speak to it, I was impressed by the comprehensive area covered by the hon. member. As he himself mentioned, I think all members are much concerned with the treatment of animals and also with the future wildlife of our country.
Along with this, Mr. Speaker, we have very deep and real concern about assuring the people of our country of the opportunity to live and continue to live a good life. When the hon. member referred to the vast and extensive file that he has on record, he reminded me of the fable of Pandora's box and I kept wondering just what was inside his file. I was hoping that perhaps we were going to be allowed to view some of the material he has in this heavy file. However, if the file were opened perhaps, like Pandora's box, it might cause more harm than good.
I did hope while he was speaking that the house would give this resolution deep and serious consideration because it deals with a matter which is important and of interest to us all. I hesitate to agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East in his suggestion that the question be referred to the committee on agriculture, because certainly some of the matters mentioned are better dealt with by other committees. The seal fishery is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) and at the present time is well regulated by that department.
The problem of disappearing species, both of bird and of animal life, is something that has been with us since the start of the world. Of course we no longer have the dinosaur or the other large animals; due to the change in world conditions they have long since ceased to exist. On the other hand we have had an increase in certain types of animals which perhaps were not so numerous in the past.
The question raised by the hon. member concerning the use of animals for medical
fMr. Cowan.]
research is one which is of concern to all of us. The question whether or not animals should be used for medical research is perhaps easy to answer; I think that if medical science is to advance at all such research is a necessity. Transplanting of organs from one dog to another took place long before it was tried with humans. There have been many amazing cases over the past years when knowledge gained from experiments with animals has been used for the furtherance of mankind and to save lives.
