speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member reminds me of insulin, a very important discovery.
I should like to comment a little further on the third item in the resolution which deals with the most humane method of trapping furbearing animals, and also asks for consideration of whether the Canadian seal hunt should and could on a practicable basis be discontinued. Although the hon. member stated that he had no particular feeling one way or the other on these items, his suggestion that the seal hunt be discontinued grates on me because I feel very strongly that it plays a vital part in the Canadian economy.
First with regard to the trapping of furbearing animals, while this is a matter to be considered by manufacturers of the traps and also by the trappers taking fur, 1 doubt whether the agriculture committee-and I do not see the connection between the agriculture committee and the trappers in our northern lands-could improve on the method used. The furs that are trapped in my area have been reduced in number over the past years, as has the number of people engaged in trapping. Nevertheless I think it is still well recognized that the Labrador mink is the best and that the quality of Labrador mink is superior to other varieties.
With reference to the seal fishery, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's suggestion that this can be discontinued on a practicable basis amazes me. The whole idea seems impossible to me and I should like to make a few points to illustrate why. The Canadian seal hunt is, of course, tied in with seal hunts in other parts of the world. In various sections of his speech the hon. member for Vancouver East referred to information he has received from many countries of the world regarding other aspects of the treatment of animals, both as pets and for use in research.
December 20, 1967

I think the Canadian seal fishery is basically divided into three areas that call for consideration. The first geographic area is the gulf, where the whitecoats are taken. The seal fishery in the gulf is limited to the whitecoats and this is closely supervised. Method of killing and quantity taken are controlled by federal government regulations. The amount is set each year and reviewed each year on the basis of size of herds. Over the past years the limit has been kept to 50,000 pelts, and at the present time this appears to be a reasonable quantity so as to maintain the seal fishery in the gulf. Should the herd become depleted the amount would be lowered; should the herd increase in number by an unwarranted amount then the limit would be increased.
The reason for controlling the number of seals taken in the gulf is based on the point made so well by the hon. member for Vancouver East, namely that we must conserve our wild animals, our fish, our birds, indeed wildlife in general in the country. The method of taking seals in the gulf is designed to conserve what is a vital industry to the area. The seals come down to this area to whelp and to breed and are there for a period of 75 days. During this time they are feeding for about 60 days, and in this wild feeding the adult seals eat about 15 pounds of fish a day. If 50,000 seals fed themselves at the rate of 15 pounds of fish a day each, this would have a direct effect on the fishery industry in the gulf area. This would affect fishermen along the coast of Quebec, and Newfoundland, and the other maritime provinces. The industry in the gulf supports approximately 40,000 men. That is not a matter that can be lightly dismissed.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
In addition, if seals were not taken in the gulf, they would eat large quantities of fish. That would have a direct effect on the fish that could be taken by our fishermen. The seals that come south also carry an enzyme or disease which attacks herring. If the seal herds were left unchecked, this disease would attack our herring schools and the herring that could be caught would be reduced. All this comes back again to the question of conservation and the balance of nature.
It is all very well to say that if nothing were taken from the sea nature would balance the seal fishery and the growth of other species of fish. But the balance of nature is
Research
not left to take place unchecked. Other species of fish are taken from the sea, and they will continue and should continue to be taken. If we did not control the seal herd we would thus reduce the amount of fish that could be taken by our fishermen in the area. In addition, sports fishing in our rivers would be affected since seals, by multiplying, would not find sufficient fish to catch at sea and would come up our rivers to attack and eat our sports fish.
The second area of sealing with which we ought to be concerned is the area of seals which are taken from the shore by fishermen who live on the shore. This area of the seal fishery involves a large area and a great number of men. The income that each individual obtains from this aspect of the seal fishery is not as great as the income of a sealer who goes to the front in a larger vessel to catch seal. At this time I am talking about those fishermen who take seals from the shore. This activity involves the province of Newfoundland and the Labrador coast; it involves also the province of Quebec in its coastal areas and certain areas of the maritime provinces where fishermen take seal from the shore to supplement their income.
The shore fishermen, if there is ice, go over that ice to take seals. If there is open water between the ice and the shore they go off in small boats through the ice in order to get at the seals. The number of seals that they take is not large; the amount of income is not large and these fishermen work hard and often risk their lives in this hard method of earning a living.
This fishery means a great deal to those fishermen at this time of year. The few seals they take mean a great deal to them. The fishery supplies them with meat from the body of the seal, and with furs, which are sold. It also brings in a small amount of income at a time of year when many fishermen have no other income. Thus it is of vital importance to them. The income they derive, at a time when other types of fishery bring them no income, is used in the spring of the year to outfit them for the summer fishery. Thus, taking seals from the shore is of vital importance to our fishermen, since the fishery provides them with food and with income with which to outfit themselves for the summer fishery.
The third aspect of the seal hunt that should be considered is the well known and well publicized seal hunt which is commonly called "at the front". Larger vessels come to

Mr. Speaker, though the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat displayed great knowledge of and interest in aspects of the seal fishery, I hope that the fact that he has made a speech does not mean that the government will not look with sympathy on this notice of motion. Speaking for the official opposition, I wish to add my full support to the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). Knowing the hon. member, as I do, I am convinced that such a motion has been presented before parliament strictly because of his concern, as a human being, for the well being of the domestic and wild animals of this country. I do not think it is put forward in the hope of any political gain which might derive from it, and in these circumstances I cannot but give my full support to this proposal, one which is put forward from the heart as this seems to be.
Turning now to the affairs of this house and the request that this subject be placed before the committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development, let me say at once that out of sheer desperation I would support any reasonable request for a subject to be discussed by this committee, in the hope that the committee might be reconstituted, especially at a time when agriculture is in such dire straits. We on the opposition side of this chamber are becoming very impatient-tired of sitting on our hands simply because the government declines to refer anything to the standing committee on agriculture to enable us to get on with the business of this great industry.
It is not my intention to repeat the arguments so ably put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver East, nor is it my intention to prolong my part in this debate. I would prefer to give the house an opportunity to arrive at a decision on this issue. I am sympathetic toward the motion because it has been presented in the fairest way in which a motion could be presented, that is to say, it does not take sides; it merely asks that the matter should be considered and that the
December 20, 1967

committee in its wisdom, after hearing witnesses, should then propose to the government what action it feels should be taken.
There is no doubt that the public conscience is seized of the way in which animals are treated in this nation. The humane society has been doing tremendous work and has been expending tremendous energy trying to focus public attention on cases of ill treatment which might otherwise have gone unnoticed. There is of course another side to this question. Charges which may be ill founded, or based only on rare instances are often made against individuals or sections of the population.
Under the proposal now put forward these people would have the opportunity to put their side of the question before parliament in order that they might be acquitted of any guilt or condemnation. This is why I am surprised at the attitude taken by the hon. member who has just spoken. He was seemingly preoccupied by a desire to protect the sealers and those who make a living from this particular industry, but I believe that if he were really concerned, following the publicity which has been given to this issue in the last 12 months, he would be delighted at the prospect of a forum which would hear both sides and before which all points of view would be put forward for the benefit of parliament.
I feel that the standing committee on agriculture is the very forum in which these matters could properly be considered. This is tied in with measures to conserve fish, birds and animal wildlife. Especially I should like the committee to deal with a subject which I believe is of great concern to the people of this nation, namely the use of chemicals in the agriculture industry for the control of noxious weds and insects, and the effect of such use upon domestic animals, wildlife, birds and fish.
Such a study might enable us to decide whether we are permitting mass murder by the use of such chemicals, wiping out species which are really of special benefit to us. It might also help us to determine whether there are residues from such chemicals which seep into the soil affecting the health of human beings. The Department of Agriculture is already doing splendid work in its efforts to keep the use of such chemicals under control, and to test them before they are released for general application. But there is always a gnawing suspicion that not enough is being done. From time to time we hear of accidents, perhaps when control has

not been sufficiently exercised, as a result of which fish die by the thousands in their ponds or streams, or a particular species of bird life is destroyed over a wide area, and these losses are assessed as being the result of the use of chemicals in agriculture.
In the committee on agriculture we have a forum where these important questions could be studied. The committee would have power, as the motion puts it, to send for persons, papers and reports to help it in its deliberations.
I approve of this prospect. It would give us an opportunity to listen to the views of knowledgeable people on all aspects of this question, and to lay before the parliament of Canada sound recommendations which might clear up once and for all the suspicions to which I have referred and the conflicting claims as to what is being done and what could be done.
Instead of prolonging my remarks I intend to resume my seat in order that we may have ample time in which to pass this motion, since I think its passage would be of great benefit to the people of this country and to the wildlife which we should all appreciate so much.

Just before he resumed his seat, the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) (Mr. Danforth) told us he intended to do so in order that the house might have an opportunity to deal with the motion before us. He seemed to forget that one of the prerogatives of members who sit in this chamber is the opportunity to speak out on subjects which concern them.
I intend to say a few words with regard to this motion the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has put forward today. Before doing so I should like to acknowledge the spirit in which he made his observations. I understand his concern. However, I am not sure that this particular notice of motion as worded would secure the results he has in mind.
Looking at the motion I see it refers to the use of animals for medical research purposes, the treatment of animals as pets, the most humane method of trapping furbearing animals, and so on. The notice of motion also refers to the Canadian seal hunt and to consideration of the entire picture relative to the maintenance of fish, bird and animal wildlife and the regulations required for conservation. I am sorry that it does not refer to two other matters which affect Canadian animals.

I refer to animals used for commercial purposes and the manner in which commercial slaughterhouses treat them. Like most hon. members I have visited slaughterhouses, and I have been appalled with the conditions under which cattle, sheep and fowl are treated in them. Yet tonight, before the evening is out, there will be hardly any of us in this house who will not sit down and partake of the flesh of animals which in many cases were not humanely slaughtered.
The notice of motion does not deal with hunters-people who participate in the sport of hunting birds, deer, caribou and other big game. I think that in hunting there is probably more cruelty than there is in the treatment of animals for medical research purposes, or than there is in the treatment of pets. I recall being invited to joint a hunt a number of years back, not far from Ottawa. When we took off early in the morning the idea was to stake out a deer. Being rather fortunate, or unfortunate on that particular day, we came across the tracks of a deer. The party of about 12 or 14 people split up and took off across farmers' fields.
Suddenly a deer, or what appeared to be a deer, shot across a field. Mr. Speaker, it sounded like the Battle of Britain all over again. Rifles and shotguns were being discharged in all directions. At the end of the shoot, fortunately there was the same number of hunters as before it started. The group I was with took off to see if it could find the deer. Unfortunately someone had hit the deer, but where, I have no idea. There was a trail of blood as far as we could follow it, until we reached water. Whether or not the deer was seriously wounded or ended up with a little bit of buckshot in it, I cannot tell.
I admire the spirit of the hon. member's proposal, but I think we should take into consideration all aspects of cruelty to animals. The third section of the hon. member's motion deals with the most humane method of trapping furbearing animals. I believe only the best possible traps should be used by Canadian and other trappers.
When a trapper takes off through the bush and sets his traps, he sets them at certain distances apart, according to his knowledge of the terrain. Then he leaves the set traps for one, two, three or four days. He returns to his trap line after one, two, three or four days, hopeful of finding mink, lynx and muskrat in his traps. The traps are designed so that the animals may be killed immediately when the traps are sprung, in order that the fur of the animals will not be destroyed.
In talking about furbearing animals I think we must take a hard look at the effect of the fur trade on certain parts of the Canadian economy, particularly the economy of the Indian and Eskimo people. Trapping is a rather hazardous occupation. It is one that produces rewards only with hard work. The price of fur varies in wild gyrations. We have had an example of this with respect to sealskins.
Until the unfortunate publicity arose over the seal hunting in the Gulf of St. Lawrence the price of sealskins, which has a direct bearing on the economy of the Eskimo people in the Arctic, averaged in the vicinity of $18 to $24 per skin. Today one can go into the Arctic and buy good sealskins for $2 or $4 each. This publicity has had a fantastic and most unfortunate effect on the economy of the Arctic. I do not suggest there is any relationship between the seal hunt in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the manner in which seals are hunted and trapped in the Arctic.
